title: Architecture Cross-Cutting Scenarios
scopeHtml: Mixed-layer incidents and design calls (ViewModel, repository, DI, navigation, build, KMP) where the answer needs several chunks at once. About 85% scenarios.

questions.promptHtml: For a typical MVVM + Hilt + Navigation Compose app, which pieces of state survive a rotation, which survive process death, and which survive neither?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Half of the architecture bugs in production are "works on my device" bugs caused by confusing these three lifetimes. It tests whether you hold a mental matrix, not a slogan.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Rotation destroys the Activity but keeps the process, so ViewModels, @Singleton objects and @ActivityRetainedScoped objects survive. Process death kills everything in memory; only what went through saved instance state (SavedStateHandle, rememberSaveable, the nav back stack and its route arguments) or disk (Room, DataStore) comes back. Anything held only in a plain field, a Singleton or a ViewModel property is gone, and the app is recreated into a screen that expects that state to exist."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Android keeps three lifetimes that people blur:

Event                 Activity/Fragment  ViewModel  Singleton/App scope  SavedState/Bundle  Disk
Rotation (config chg)   recreated         KEPT        KEPT                 KEPT               KEPT
Back out of screen      destroyed         cleared     KEPT                 dropped            KEPT
Process death           gone              GONE        GONE                 RESTORED*          KEPT
User swipes from recents (force-stop)     GONE        GONE                 GONE (not restored) KEPT

* Restored only when the system killed the process while the task was in the background. A user-initiated swipe-away or a force stop discards saved state, so do not rely on it for correctness, only for continuity.

Mechanism: ViewModelStore is retained across configuration change by the ComponentActivity through NonConfigurationInstances, which lives in the process. A dead process loses it. SavedStateHandle is backed by the SavedStateRegistry, which is serialized into the Bundle in onSaveInstanceState, so it is subject to Binder transaction limits (about 1 MB shared across the whole process transaction; keep per-screen state to a few KB).

Design rule: every screen must be reconstructable from (route arguments + SavedStateHandle + disk/network). Whatever is in-memory only must be treated as a cache.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@HiltViewModel
class CheckoutViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val savedState: SavedStateHandle,
    private val cart: CartRepository,          // reads from disk, so it survives
) : ViewModel() {
    // survives process death: small, primitive, restorable
    val couponCode: StateFlow<String> = savedState.getStateFlow("coupon", "")

    // survives rotation only: rebuild from repository after process death
    val uiState: StateFlow<CheckoutUi> = cart.observeCart()
        .map(::toUi)
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), CheckoutUi.Loading)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Testing only rotation. Use "Don't keep activities" or adb shell am kill <pkg> after backgrounding the app to test process death.
  • Storing a whole domain object list in SavedStateHandle (TransactionTooLargeException).
  • Assuming a @Singleton "session" object is still populated after the app returns from background.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you reproduce process death locally? → Background the app, then adb shell am kill com.example.app, reopen from recents. Or enable Developer options "Don't keep activities" (this tests Activity recreation, not full process death).
  2. Is rememberSaveable the same as SavedStateHandle? → Both use the saved-state mechanism; rememberSaveable is composition-scoped UI state, SavedStateHandle is ViewModel-scoped.
  3. What happens to an in-flight network request on process death? → It is gone; the restored screen must re-issue it, which implies idempotent loads and for writes a persisted outbox.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "ViewModel survives rotation, not process death." Senior: gives the full matrix, names the Bundle size limit, explains that the architecture should make memory a cache of disk/arguments, and describes how they test it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A crash spike of lateinit property has not been initialized only on low-RAM devices after backgrounding is the classic signature of in-memory-only state assumed to exist on restore.

questions.contextHtml:
A payments screen shows a "Payment failed" snackbar. QA: "On rotation during the request, the snackbar sometimes never appears. Also when I press Home, wait for the failure, then come back, nothing is shown." Crash-free rate is fine; it is a silent bug. Code:

class PayViewModel(private val repo: PayRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<PayEvent>()   // replay = 0
    val events = _events.asSharedFlow()

    fun pay() = viewModelScope.launch {
        repo.pay().onFailure { _events.emit(PayEvent.ShowError(it.message)) }
    }
}

// Activity
override fun onCreate(s: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(s)
    lifecycleScope.launch { vm.events.collect { show(it) } }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find why the event is lost, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use LiveData / SingleLiveEvent instead." That reintroduces the original problem (events delivered to nobody or twice) and does not explain why this SharedFlow drops.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the event purely transient UI (snackbar) or must it be acted on (navigate after payment)? That decides drop-tolerance. Which min SDK / lifecycle library is used? Is the screen Compose or Views?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix that shows the failure as state, since payment failure that the user never sees is a trust issue.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) MutableSharedFlow() with no replay and no buffer drops emissions when there are zero subscribers; (b) the collector is not lifecycle-aware, so on rotation there is a window with no collector; (c) collecting in lifecycleScope.launch keeps collecting while STOPPED (a different bug: UI touched in background).
  4. How I'd verify: Add a log inside emit and collect; reproduce with "Don't keep activities" and a throttled network. Unit test with Turbine: emit before collection starts and assert nothing arrives.
  5. Root cause: A SharedFlow with replay = 0 and no extraBufferCapacity delivers only to current subscribers; with none, emit returns immediately and the value is discarded. On rotation the Activity is recreated, the old collector is cancelled and the new one is not yet subscribed. Backgrounding: the collector in lifecycleScope.launch is still active when STOPPED in this example, but if one adds repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) to be safe, the same gap appears.
  6. Fix: Short term: make the failure state, which is what the official guidance prefers (reduce events to UI state, verify current wording on developer.android.com UI events page):
data class PayUi(val loading: Boolean = false, val errorMessage: String? = null)

fun pay() = viewModelScope.launch {
    _ui.update { it.copy(loading = true) }
    repo.pay().onFailure { e -> _ui.update { it.copy(loading = false, errorMessage = e.message) } }
}
fun errorShown() = _ui.update { it.copy(errorMessage = null) }

UI shows the snackbar when errorMessage != null and calls errorShown() after. Long term: if a Channel is truly needed, Channel<PayEvent>(Channel.BUFFERED) exposed with receiveAsFlow() and collected under repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED); know that an element received just as the collector is cancelled can still be lost. 7. Prevention: Convention: ViewModels never expose MutableSharedFlow without a documented drop policy; a test that emits before subscription and across repeatOnLifecycle restart. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use replay = 1 as a fix: the event replays on every re-collection (snackbar reappears after rotation). Event-as-state needs an explicit "consumed" call, which is more code but loses nothing.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the "event" is navigate-to-receipt after success? → Model it as state (receiptId != null) and have the UI navigate then call onNavigated(); navigating twice is worse than a missed snackbar.
  • Why not just Channel.UNLIMITED? → Unbounded memory if nobody ever collects and stale events delivered much later.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team fixed "lost toast" with replay = 1; two weeks later support got reports of old error toasts reappearing after rotating the phone on unrelated screens. The real fix was state plus acknowledgment.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests SingleLiveEvent or sleeps/delays emission.
  • Hire: Identifies zero-subscriber drop and fixes with state or Channel under repeatOnLifecycle.
  • Strong hire: Also explains Channel cancellation edge case, replay trap, and what is drop-tolerant versus must-handle.

questions.contextHtml:
Android crash and memory dashboard: OOM rate rose from 0.2% to 0.9% of sessions on 3 GB RAM devices after release 7.4. LeakCanary in a debug build shows: GC ROOT static Hilt SingletonComponent -> ImageUploader.activityContext -> MainActivity (leaked). 40 MB retained per leaked Activity instance, and users rotate often. The diff in 7.4:

@Singleton
class ImageUploader @Inject constructor(
    @ActivityContext private val activityContext: Context   // added so it can show a progress dialog
) { ... }

Hilt was happy and the build passed, because the project applies an old workaround.
questions.promptHtml: Why did this leak, what is the correct fix, and how do you stop it recurring?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use applicationContext and add a null check." Treats symptom; does not address that the class is doing UI from a singleton.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the uploader need to outlive the Activity (a long upload)? Does it genuinely need UI? Is @ActivityContext actually resolvable in SingletonComponent in this build (it normally is not, so which workaround is in play?).
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the constructor change or hot-patch to use @ApplicationContext and drop the dialog; stage rollout back to previous percent.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A longer-lived scope holds a shorter-lived object (Singleton holds Activity); (b) a lambda/callback registered on the singleton captures the Activity; (c) a coroutine in an app scope captures the view.
  4. How I'd verify: LeakCanary's leak trace (already points at the field), then grep for @ActivityContext in @Singleton classes, then heap dump in Android Studio Profiler and filter MainActivity instance count after 5 rotations.
  5. Root cause: Object lifetime inversion. SingletonComponent lives for the process; the Activity is destroyed on each rotation, but the singleton still references the first instance. Hilt normally rejects this: @ActivityContext is only bound in ActivityComponent and below, so injecting it into a @Singleton should fail with a [Dagger/MissingBinding]. Here the project had a manual @Provides @ActivityContext in a @InstallIn(SingletonComponent) module, which defeated the guardrail (verify the actual compile error in your Hilt version).
  6. Fix: Short term: inject @ApplicationContext and expose upload progress as a StateFlow; the screen renders the dialog. Long term: UI concerns never go into data-layer singletons:
@Singleton
class ImageUploader @Inject constructor(@ApplicationContext private val ctx: Context) {
    private val _progress = MutableStateFlow(0)
    val progress: StateFlow<Int> = _progress.asStateFlow()
}
  1. Prevention: Delete the bogus module; a Konsist/lint rule "no Activity/Context subtype fields in @Singleton classes"; LeakCanary in the debug build plus an instrumentation test that rotates and asserts no retained Activity.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use WeakReference<Activity> as a patch; it hides the design error and produces dialogs that silently never show.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• When is a Singleton holding a Context fine? → Only the application context.
  • Why 40 MB per Activity? → The Activity retains its view hierarchy and bitmaps, so one leak is a lot; N rotations multiply it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A leak looked like "bitmap bloat" for a week because the heap showed only large Bitmap objects. Following the path to GC root found one singleton callback.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "Add System.gc()" or WeakReference.
  • Hire: Names scope inversion and moves to app context plus state.
  • Strong hire: Also explains why Hilt should have blocked it and adds a rule so it cannot return.

questions.contextHtml:
A 6-engineer team has 14 repositories, 11 of which look like this. A new hire opens a PR deleting them: "pure boilerplate, call the API directly from the ViewModel." Two seniors disagree. Stats: each repository change touches 3 files (interface, impl, fake); the app has 40 screens; one backend migration last year changed 2 of the 14 endpoints.

interface UserRepository { suspend fun getUser(id: String): UserDto }
class UserRepositoryImpl(private val api: UserApi) : UserRepository {
    override suspend fun getUser(id: String) = api.getUser(id)
}
questions.promptHtml: Do you delete them? What is your position and how do you settle it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Repositories are best practice, never remove them" or "all abstraction is waste." Both are dogma.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does any repository cache, merge sources, map errors, or enforce threading? Do tests rely on fakes? Do DTOs reach the UI? Is there a plan for offline?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; it is not an incident. I'd hold the PR for a short design discussion rather than merge in either direction.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Pass-through repos currently add only indirection; (b) but they are the only seam where DTO to domain mapping and error mapping would live; (c) removal increases the cost of the next backend change since DTOs would be referenced from 40 screens.
  4. How I'd verify: Count the references to *Dto in ViewModels and UI; count tests using the fakes; check git history for which repositories changed in the last 12 months.
  5. Root cause: The repository was adopted as a ritual rather than for a job. Its job is to own data semantics: source selection, caching, mapping, errors. Pass-through repos do none of it, so the only value left is a test seam.
  6. Fix: Be selective. Keep a repository where it maps DTO to domain or merges/caches. For a pure pass-through, a ViewModel may call a thin interface directly, but do not leak DTOs to the UI: put a mapper at the boundary. Merge the "interface + impl + fake" trio to the minimum: interface only where a fake is used by tests.
  7. Prevention: A documented rule in the architecture decision record: "Create a repository when there is a second source, a cache, a mapping or an error policy; otherwise a data source or API interface is allowed to be injected directly." Review checklist item.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not mass-delete 11 files in one PR; I'd convert as screens are touched. I'd not keep UserDto visible to composables under any option, because the next backend rename then breaks 40 screens.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if offline mode is on the roadmap in a quarter? → Keep repos for entities that will be cached; adding them later is cheap if DTOs were not leaked.
  • Does Google's guidance require repositories? → The official guide describes the data layer in terms of repositories, but the domain layer is optional; judge by the job.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team deleted pass-through repos, then six months later a backend field rename touched 60 composables. They reintroduced mappers only.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Pure dogma either way.
  • Hire: Defines the repository's job and proposes selective removal.
  • Strong hire: Adds measurable criteria, the DTO leak risk, and an incremental plan with an ADR.

questions.contextHtml: HomeViewModel is 2,300 lines, 31 constructor parameters, 14 StateFlows, three init blocks launching coroutines. Home gets 70% of sessions, 1.2M DAU. Release cadence is weekly with 20% staged rollouts. Last quarter 4 of 9 Home bugs were regressions from unrelated edits (a change to the carousel broke the banner). Unit tests: 0 for this class because the constructor cannot be built without 31 fakes. PM refuses a feature freeze.
questions.promptHtml: How do you decompose this without stopping feature work or breaking Home?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Rewrite it with MVI in a new branch." Big-bang rewrite with no safety net on the highest-traffic screen.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which sections of Home are independent (carousel, banners, continue-watching, search)? Which share state? How many engineers touch it per sprint? Is there a screenshot or UI test harness?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add characterization tests around the most regression-prone paths first, and freeze new init work: new Home features go into new holders, never into the god class.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Sections are independently loadable and loosely coupled, so a split by section works; (b) hidden coupling via shared mutable state (selected tab, user profile); (c) init ordering dependencies.
  4. How I'd verify: Draw the dependency map: for each StateFlow, who writes and who reads. Count writers per field. Use a coverage run and Studio's "Find usages" to cluster methods by field.
  5. Root cause: No seam, so every feature appended to the same class; the constructor became a service locator.
  6. Fix: Strangler by section. Step 1: extract a pure HomeSectionState per section and a plain Kotlin state holder class (not a ViewModel) with its own scope-taking constructor. Step 2: HomeViewModel delegates and combines:
class HomeViewModel @Inject constructor(
    carousel: CarouselHolder, banners: BannersHolder, continueWatching: ContinueHolder,
) : ViewModel() {
    val ui: StateFlow<HomeUi> = combine(carousel.state, banners.state, continueWatching.state, ::HomeUi)
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), HomeUi.Loading)
}

One section per PR, each behind its existing UI so the screen does not change. Step 3: the composable for each section may then take its own holder. 7. Prevention: A file-size/constructor-param lint warning (e.g. detekt LongParameterList, class size), CODEOWNERS per section, ViewModel unit tests per holder. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not split into one ViewModel per section prematurely (shared scope and parent-child coordination become harder); I'd not introduce a new architecture style at the same time as the extraction.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two sections share the "selected profile" state. → Lift it into a small shared holder injected into both, owned by the parent; do not let sections reference each other.
  • How do you roll out safely? → Staged 20% rollout with crash and section-render-failure metrics compared against baseline.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The refactor took 7 PRs over 5 weeks; every PR was behavior-neutral and shipped in the normal train. The only incident was an init ordering assumption, which the characterization test caught.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Big rewrite.
  • Hire: Incremental extraction with tests.
  • Strong hire: Characterization tests first, holder (not ViewModel) extraction, shared-state lift, and metric-gated rollout.

questions.contextHtml:
Crash dashboard shows a new top crash after release 8.1: java.lang.IllegalStateException: ProductDetail requires product ... TransactionTooLargeException: data parcel size 1,048,204 bytes in a smaller group (about 3% of crashes, mostly low-RAM devices, always after the user backgrounded the app for several minutes). Release 8.1 changed navigation to type-safe routes (Navigation 2.8+):

@Serializable
data class ProductDetail(val product: ProductUi)   // product has description (4 KB), 12 images, reviews list

Instrumented flows in QA pass.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose it and explain the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make ProductUi Parcelable" or "increase heap." Misreads the failure as a type problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How big is a typical ProductUi payload? Do crashes correlate with a particular screen depth? Is the crash at save time (background) or restore time (foreground)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the 8.1 route change via staged rollout halt; if impossible, patch to pass only the id.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The whole object is serialized into the destination's arguments Bundle and persisted in onSaveInstanceState; large args times several back stack entries exceed the ~1 MB Binder limit; (b) restore path reads null because the route class could not be restored; (c) a changed @Serializable class between versions breaking restore after an app update (red herring here because crashes are within the same version).
  4. How I'd verify: Log Bundle sizes with a debug helper in onSaveInstanceState; reproduce with adb shell am kill after navigating 4 screens deep; Studio Profiler memory check is a red herring since heap is fine.
  5. Root cause: Arguments live in the back stack entry and are saved with the saved instance state. State saved there is transported in a transaction shared by the whole process; the sum for the whole stack crossed about 1 MB. Passing the data object turned a navigation key into a data store.
  6. Fix: Route carries only the identifier; the destination's ViewModel loads data from the repository (disk cache first), which also fixes staleness:
@Serializable data class ProductDetail(val productId: String)

@HiltViewModel
class ProductVM @Inject constructor(
    savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle, repo: ProductRepository,
) : ViewModel() {
    private val id = savedStateHandle.toRoute<ProductDetail>().productId
    val ui = repo.observeProduct(id).stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), null)
}
  1. Prevention: A lint/Konsist rule "route classes contain only primitives, enums or small value types"; a debug-build assertion that logs when saved state exceeds ~200 KB; QA checklist includes process-death run.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not cache the object in a static map (dies with the process, same failure). I'd not catch TransactionTooLargeException; it surfaces in the framework path.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Shared element needs the title instantly. → Pass the title as a small display hint arg and still load by id.
  • Many entries in the stack: how big is too big? → Keep the whole app's saved state well under a few hundred KB; verify measurement per app.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The same bug appeared with a SavedStateHandle holding a filter list; fixed by persisting to DataStore and storing a version token.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Changes types or adds Parcelable.
  • Hire: Pass id, load in ViewModel.
  • Strong hire: Explains Binder limit, back-stack multiplication, and adds guards.

questions.contextHtml: An e-commerce app has a cart tab and a product screen. Support tickets: "Added an item, cart badge says 2, cart screen shows 1 item for a few seconds, sometimes forever." 1 in 400 sessions. Architecture: the cart screen's ViewModel keeps a MutableStateFlow<List<CartItem>> loaded once in init; the product screen's ViewModel calls cartRepo.add(item) (which writes to Room and calls the API). The badge reads from Room; the cart screen reads the list loaded at init. Bottom navigation keeps the cart ViewModel alive via nav-graph scoping. Logs: add ok, no errors.
questions.promptHtml: Why is state stale, and how do you design it so it cannot be?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Call refresh() in onResume." A band-aid that polls instead of fixing ownership.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the cart live on the server or locally first? Does bottom-nav retain the ViewModel? Any other writers to the cart (push, other device)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cheap guard: reload when the cart tab is selected so users stop seeing stale lists, while the real fix is prepared.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Two sources of truth: the badge observes Room, the screen holds a one-time copy; (b) ViewModel retained for the whole nav-graph so init ran once; (c) a race where API response overwrites newer local state.
  4. How I'd verify: Log writer/reader per source; reproduce by adding an item while cart tab was loaded earlier; Room Inspector to confirm the DB is correct (it is).
  5. Root cause: Snapshot-in-ViewModel instead of observing the single source of truth. The data was right in Room; the cart ViewModel copied it once and never subscribed again.
  6. Fix:
class CartViewModel(repo: CartRepository) : ViewModel() {
    val items: StateFlow<List<CartItem>> = repo.observeCart()   // Room Flow
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyList())
}

Both the badge and the screen derive from observeCart(); mutations go through repository functions only. 7. Prevention: Rule: ViewModels expose derived flows from repository flows, not loaded-once lists, for data that other screens can change; a test that mutates the repository and asserts the screen state updates without any lifecycle event. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not use a shared event bus ("CartUpdated") because a missed event leaves stale state with no recovery. I'd not share one ViewModel between the two screens only to share data; share the repository.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two-device edits? → Server is truth; use sync with versioning, local Room reflects merged result.
  • What if the API write fails after local optimistic add? → Roll back with a pending flag and surface a retry.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "refresh on resume" patch hid the bug for a quarter; then a background push changed the cart and the stale list reappeared.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: onResume refresh.
  • Hire: Single source of truth observed via Flow.
  • Strong hire: Rejects event bus, explains conflicts and optimistic rollback.

questions.promptHtml: A bug report comes in that smells architectural (stale data, lost event, crash only after backgrounding). What is your triage ladder, and what do you check in what order?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors are hired for fast, structured diagnosis across layers instead of guessing at the layer they know best.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I ask four questions in order: lifetime (which scope owns this object and does it outlive its consumer?), source of truth (how many copies of this state exist?), delivery (is this a state or an event, and can it be dropped or duplicated?), and thread/time (who runs this and when?). Then I reproduce with the cheapest forcing function: rotation, process kill, slow network, logout, or low memory."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Symptom                         First suspect            Forcing function
Works then wrong after bg       process death            adb shell am kill
Wrong only after rotate         non-retained state/event "Don't keep activities", rotate
Old user's data shown           scope outlives session   logout then login as another user
Stale across screens            copies of state          mutate in screen A, observe B
Rare, per-device                threading/race           StrictMode, slow device, repeat 100x
Build/CI only                   graph/config             --scan, module graph

Mechanism: most architecture bugs are mismatches between lifetimes (scope A holds something that scope B owns), copies (two truths), or delivery semantics (one-shot versus durable). Naming the mismatch gives the fix: align scope, make one owner and observe it, or convert events to state.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// A cheap guard that makes lifetime mismatches loud in debug builds
if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) {
    StrictMode.setVmPolicy(
        StrictMode.VmPolicy.Builder().detectLeakedClosableObjects().detectActivityLeaks().penaltyLog().build()
    )
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Fixing the symptom layer (UI refresh) instead of ownership.
  • Reproducing only on a fast emulator with Wi-Fi.
  • Adding logs after the fix, not before, so you cannot prove the cause.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What do you instrument first? → Creation/clear of the suspect scope and writes to the suspect state.
  2. How do you prove the fix? → A regression test that applies the forcing function (e.g. recreate, restore, logout).
  3. How do you stop the class of bug? → A lint/architecture rule or a base abstraction making the wrong thing impossible.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE debugs inside the screen. Senior classifies by lifetime/ownership/delivery/time and picks a forcing function.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Classifying "the cart shows an old user's item" as scope-outlives-session cut a week of UI-layer debugging to an hour.

questions.contextHtml: A fintech app with 900k DAU. Incident: a user on a shared family tablet logged out of Account A and into Account B and saw A's balance for about 2 seconds, then B's. Security flagged it as P1. Logs on the device: logout complete then GET /balance 200 for B. In code, @Singleton class AccountRepository holds MutableStateFlow<Balance> and a @Singleton class AuthTokenHolder. Logout clears tokens and navigates to login, but the Singleton BalanceStore keeps its last value; the ViewModel of the first nav entry started collecting the cached flow before the fresh request returned.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: root cause, fix, and structural prevention.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Clear the balance on logout." Fixes one field; the next singleton added will leak again.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many singletons hold user-scoped data? Does the app support multiple accounts without logout? Is there on-disk user data (Room, DataStore) per user? What is the data-protection requirement?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: on logout, clear the known stores and show a loading state until the new user's data arrives; additionally process-restart after logout as an emergency blunt tool.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) User-scoped data lives in process-scoped singletons; (b) logout is an imperative list of clear() calls someone forgot to extend; (c) DB and prefs are not keyed per user; (d) caches in HTTP layer (OkHttp cache) are shared.
  4. How I'd verify: Inventory every @Singleton and classify user-scoped vs app-scoped (grep, Hilt component tree from the generated code); write an instrumented test: login A, load data, logout, login B, assert nothing from A is emitted at any point; check OkHttp cache and image caches.
  5. Root cause: User identity is not a scope. Lifetime of user data (a session) is shorter than the Singleton, and cleanup relies on discipline.
  6. Fix: Short term: a SessionCleaner that all user-scoped singletons register with (fun onLogout()), plus clear Room/DataStore for the user and the HTTP cache. Long term: a session-scoped container created at login and dropped at logout, so user data lives on an object that does not exist when logged out:
@Singleton
class SessionManager @Inject constructor(private val factory: UserSessionComponent.Factory) {
    private val _session = MutableStateFlow<UserSession?>(null)
    val session: StateFlow<UserSession?> = _session
    fun login(user: User) { _session.value = UserSession(factory.create(user)) }
    fun logout() { _session.value?.close(); _session.value = null }
}

Hilt has no custom components, so this uses a plain Dagger subcomponent or a manually built session graph hung off an @EntryPoint (verify the current guidance on custom scopes with Hilt). 7. Prevention: The Konsist/lint rule: classes holding User* types must not be @Singleton; a logout test in CI; review checklist item "who clears this on logout?"; security review for cached data on disk. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not rely only on killing the process (breaks background sync handoff and is hostile UX). I would not make everything session-scoped; app config and feature flags are app-scoped.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Account switching without logout (A and B both logged in)? → Session map keyed by user id; one active session; background work captures its own session.
  • In-flight request from A returns after logout? → Cancel the session's scope on logout; responses never write to a closed session.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The review found 17 singletons with user data; 9 had no logout path at all. The session container removed the whole class of bug.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Clears one field.
  • Hire: Inventory and a central cleanup mechanism.
  • Strong hire: Session-scoped graph, cancelled in-flight work, on-disk and HTTP cache coverage, executable guardrail.

questions.contextHtml: Build fails after a PR from the Orders team: Circular dependency between the following tasks: :feature:orders:compileDebugKotlin ... :feature:cart:compileDebugKotlin .... Orders needs CartSummary from :feature:cart, and Cart already depended on :feature:orders to open an order after checkout. The PR author added implementation(project(":feature:orders")) to :feature:cart. Main is red for the whole team (35 engineers), merge queue blocked.
questions.promptHtml: Unblock main and fix the structure.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Merge the two modules." Removes the symptom and builds a coarser monolith.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which edge is new (just revert that)? Which direction is the true dependency? Is the shared type a model or a behavior?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the offending PR to unblock main in minutes; fix forward on a branch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A feature module depends on a sibling feature rather than on a contract; (b) shared model lives in the wrong module; (c) navigation coupling (cart wants to open an order).
  4. How I'd verify: ./gradlew :feature:cart:dependencies --configuration debugCompileClasspath; a module graph plugin (verify the tool in use) to draw edges; check which symbols are actually used across the edge.
  5. Root cause: Features reference each other directly, creating a cycle. Gradle rejects cycles at task graph level, so it is loud and early (a good thing).
  6. Fix: Break the cycle with a contract module. Move CartSummary and the "open order" route into :feature:orders:api (or :core:model and :core:navigation); each feature depends on the other's api, not its impl; the app module wires implementations:
// :feature:cart/build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation(projects.feature.orders.api)   // contract only
}
// :feature:orders:api
@Serializable data class OrderDetailRoute(val orderId: String)
interface CartSummaryProvider { fun summary(): Flow<CartSummary> }

Orders gets the cart summary through an interface bound in the app module's DI graph. 7. Prevention: Enforce direction (feature impl depends only on core and other features' api) with a Gradle dependency-rule check or Konsist test in CI; PR template question "new module dependency edge?". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not use api(project(...)) to paper over it, nor merge modules; a :core:common dumping ground is the other trap since it re-couples everything.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not an event bus between features? → Hidden coupling and untestable contracts; typed interfaces are visible in the graph.
  • Does the cycle exist at the source level only? → Gradle detects module-level cycles; source-level cycles inside one module are not caught.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Four teams added "just one" cross-feature dependency each; two quarters later a layer check found 31 feature-to-feature impl edges.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Merge modules or use api().
  • Hire: Contract module with a revert first.
  • Strong hire: Adds enforcement and explains navigation contract.

questions.contextHtml: PR CI takes 25 minutes (target: under 12). Android app, 85 modules, Kotlin 2.x, AGP 8.x, KAPT in 22 modules (Hilt, Room), ephemeral CI agents with no persistent Gradle home, 40 PRs/day, 8 vCPU runners. Build scan summary: configuration 3m10s, dependency resolution/download 2m40s, compile 14m (KAPT stubs 5m), lint 3m, unit tests 2m. Local incremental builds are fine (about 40 s).
questions.promptHtml: What do you change, in what order, and how do you prove it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Bigger CI machines." Cost goes up, wall time barely moves because the work is serial and uncached.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is a remote build cache enabled? Is the config cache usable on CI (Gradle version, plugins)? Which tasks are cache misses? Are all 85 modules needed per PR?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Enable org.gradle.caching=true and org.gradle.parallel=true; set up a read/write remote build cache for main-branch CI and read-only for PRs; cache the Gradle dependency cache between runs.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Cold agents recompile everything (no remote cache); (b) KAPT dominates (stubs generation is not incremental across modules as well as KSP); (c) configuration time is high without configuration cache; (d) lint and tests run on all modules, not just affected.
  4. How I'd verify: Gradle build scan with --scan; the "Performance" tab shows cache misses by task; --profile; compare an A/B run. Change one thing per run and keep the scan URLs.
  5. Root cause: Work is both cold and unnecessarily large: nothing is reused across agents, annotation processing is slow, and tasks are not limited to what changed.
  6. Fix: In order: remote build cache plus dependency cache (biggest, lowest risk); configuration cache (org.gradle.configuration-cache=true, fix incompatible plugins); migrate KAPT to KSP for Room and Hilt where supported (verify versions: Room has KSP, Dagger/Hilt KSP support exists in recent 2.4x/2.5x, verify per version); run lint only on the changed modules or on a nightly full lint; shard unit tests. Expected result: after warm cache the scan shows most compile tasks FROM-CACHE.
# gradle.properties
org.gradle.caching=true
org.gradle.parallel=true
org.gradle.configuration-cache=true
  1. Prevention: Track CI p50/p90 time as a dashboard metric; alert on cache hit-rate drop; a build-logic check for non-cacheable tasks; periodic scans.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not enable a writable remote cache for PR builds (cache poisoning risk); I'd not skip lint entirely, only move the full run off the critical path.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cache hit rate stays at 40%. → Look for non-deterministic inputs (timestamps, absolute paths, BuildConfig time) that change task inputs.
  • Config cache breaks a plugin. → Pin or replace the plugin; use --configuration-cache-problems=warn while triaging.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A buildConfigField with a git timestamp invalidated 60 modules' caches on every commit.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Bigger machines.
  • Hire: Remote cache, KSP, scan-based measurement.
  • Strong hire: Order by impact, cache poisoning policy, and input determinism.

questions.contextHtml:
A new checkout flow crashes for 6% of users on one OEM. The team flips the Firebase Remote Config kill switch at 10:05. At 12:30 crash rate is still 5.4%. The code:

class FlagRepo(private val rc: FirebaseRemoteConfig) {
    init { rc.setConfigSettingsAsync(remoteConfigSettings { minimumFetchIntervalInSeconds = 43_200 }) }
    suspend fun refresh() { rc.fetchAndActivate().await() }
    fun newCheckout(): Boolean = rc.getBoolean("new_checkout")
}
// refresh() called once in Application.onCreate

Many affected users are in the subway or on bad networks; app processes stay alive for days.
questions.promptHtml: Why did the kill switch not work and how do you redesign it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Lower the fetch interval to 0." Violates throttling guidance and does nothing for already-running processes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What fraction have fetched since 10:05? Are flags read at app start only? Is there a staged rollout/force-update lever? Does the crash happen before flags load?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt/rollback the staged rollout in Play Console; if the server controls the flow, disable the new endpoint path server-side; push an in-app config via a higher-frequency channel if one exists.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The default minimum fetch interval is 12 hours, so clients served cached values until it elapses (the value 43,200 s here equals 12 h); (b) fetch happens only at process start, and long-lived processes never refetch; (c) fetched values are fetched but not activated until the next start; (d) the crash occurs before refresh.
  4. How I'd verify: Remote Config fetch-status logs and "last fetch time"; analytics event with flag value per session; crash dashboard segmented by app uptime and flag value.
  5. Root cause: Kill switch latency equals fetch interval plus restart cadence, which is hours to days. The flag is a configuration channel, not an emergency channel.
  6. Fix: Short term: server-side kill (backend response field or header that clients check), plus real-time Remote Config updates where supported (addOnConfigUpdateListener, verify the minimum SDK version) so activated values apply to running processes. Long term: a flag provider interface with defaults compiled in, evaluation at point of use (not cached in a field), fetch on foreground with backoff, and a separate "safety" channel with a short TTL for kill switches:
interface Flags { fun isEnabled(flag: Flag): Boolean }   // evaluated per call
fun startCheckout() = if (flags.isEnabled(Flag.NewCheckout)) newFlow() else legacyFlow()

For crash-on-launch kill switches, the process must survive them: crash-loop detection that auto-disables a flag after N crashes. 7. Prevention: Run a quarterly kill-switch drill measuring time to 95% of active devices; alert on "flag staleness p95"; every risky flag needs a compiled-in safe default. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not set the fetch interval to 0 in production (throttled by the backend and drains battery); I'd not make the safe default "new code on".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Offline user, first launch? → In-app defaults apply; the default must be the safe path.
  • Flag value must not change mid-session. → Snapshot per session for experiments, but not for kill switches.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The first real kill-switch drill reached 61% of actives in 4 hours, so the team added a server-side check to checkout start.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Lowers fetch interval.
  • Hire: Identifies fetch/activate latency and the server-side lever.
  • Strong hire: Safe defaults, real-time updates, crash-loop auto-disable, measured drills.

questions.contextHtml: Marketing sends a push campaign with deep link app://offers/123 to 2M users. Offers is an on-demand dynamic feature module (Play Feature Delivery; 4 MB). Initial test: 18% of tapped users see the app open to the Home screen and nothing happens; 4% see a crash Navigation destination ... cannot be found. Offline users and Wi-Fi-less users are common (emerging markets, 35% on metered data). Product says: "Just make it work, no extra screens."
questions.promptHtml: Design the behavior for a deep link into a module that may not be installed.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Include the module in the base APK." Ignores the explicit size trade-off and does not answer the question.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Why is Offers on-demand (APK size budget)? What fraction of users have it installed? What is acceptable latency/UX for a 4 MB download? Is there an install-time alternative?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the crash: route all deep links through a single entry in the base module that checks module install state; for unresolved links, fall back to Home plus a message.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Navigation graph destination in the dynamic module is not available until installed; (b) deep link resolved before install completes; (c) navigation after install completion races the activity recreation (split install may require recreation).
  4. How I'd verify: bundletool local testing with --local-testing to simulate install; test on a device with the module absent; check the SplitInstallManager state events.
  5. Root cause: The link target is not part of the running app, and nothing owned the install-then-navigate sequence.
  6. Fix: Base module owns a DeepLinkRouter: parse link, check splitInstallManager.installedModules, if missing show a progress state, request install, on success navigate (verify whether Navigation's dynamic features support applies to Compose in your version, otherwise implement the sequence manually), on failure show retry with a base-module web fallback screen.
suspend fun open(link: Uri) {
    if ("offers" !in manager.installedModules) {
        when (installer.request("offers")) {           // wraps SplitInstallManager listener
            Installed -> router.navigate(link)
            else -> router.navigate(Fallback.web(link)) // WebView or browser fallback
        }
    } else router.navigate(link)
}
  1. Prevention: Deep link test matrix (installed/not installed/offline); analytics funnel of tap, resolve, install, land; campaign preflight check.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not silently auto-install on metered data without a hint; I'd not move Offers into base without comparing the 4 MB cost against the conversion lift.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Link arrives while the app is cold-starting. → Hold it in a pending-intent holder that the nav host consumes after graph set up.
  • Module has been installed but process not restarted. → Some splits need recreation; verify behavior per API level.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A campaign analysis showed 40% of the tapped users never reached Offers; a fallback web view recovered a third of them.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Put it in base.
  • Hire: Install-then-navigate with a fallback.
  • Strong hire: Handles cold start, metered data policy, test matrix and funnel metrics.

questions.contextHtml: A 120-module app with hand-written Dagger 2: one AppComponent, 6 subcomponents, DaggerAppComponent built in Application, AndroidInjector-style activities, 1.5M DAU, weekly release. Goal: Hilt in 6 months, no feature freeze, crash-free must stay above 99.7%. Build-time budget: clean build must not regress by more than 10%.
questions.promptHtml: Plan the migration.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Convert everything in one branch over a weekend." No incremental path, no rollback.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many custom scopes and subcomponents? Any use of dagger-android? How are ViewModels created now? Is there a multi-process app? Why Hilt (standardization, testing, hiring)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident. First step: prove it works in one low-risk leaf screen before committing the plan.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Risks: (a) custom subcomponents not mapping to Hilt's fixed hierarchy; (b) coexistence period where two graphs provide the same binding; (c) build time from aggregation; (d) tests that build components manually.
  4. How I'd verify: Pilot module; compare build scans before/after; compile-time errors from Hilt validation; instrumented tests per migrated screen.
  5. Root cause: N/A, this is a design plan. The key insight is that Hilt generates the component tree, so coexistence means Hilt owns the application component while the legacy graph is exposed to it through an entry point or bridge.
  6. Fix (plan): Phase 0: upgrade Dagger to a version Hilt supports; add @HiltAndroidApp and Hilt plugin; keep AppComponent alive. Phase 1: bridge, expose the legacy component's bindings through @EntryPoint modules installed in SingletonComponent so new code can inject them. Phase 2: migrate screens leaf-first with @AndroidEntryPoint, replacing AndroidInjector one Activity at a time (Hilt provides @OptionalInject for gradual migration, verify the current doc). Phase 3: move modules to @InstallIn, map subcomponents to Hilt scopes (ActivityRetained, ViewModel, Fragment) or entry-point-based custom graphs. Phase 4: delete the legacy component and the bridge. Each phase is a separate release; flags are not needed since changes are behavior neutral.
@EntryPoint @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
interface LegacyBridge { fun userRepository(): UserRepository }  // legacy graph exposes via adapter module
  1. Prevention: Duplicate binding detection by compile errors; migration progress dashboard (screens migrated); ban new DaggerXComponent usage with a lint rule.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not rewrite all scopes at once; I'd not leave the bridge permanent. Cost: temporary duplicate wiring and some build-time overhead; revert path is per release.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Build time regressed 25%. → Check KAPT vs KSP, enableAggregatingTask, and modules with Hilt processors that do not need them.
  • A subcomponent per logged-in user? → Hilt has no custom components; keep a Dagger subcomponent hung off an entry point.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The migration finished in 5 months; the bridge removal was the hardest part because every module had one stray manual component reference.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Big-bang.
  • Hire: Phased with coexistence.
  • Strong hire: Entry-point bridge, scope mapping, build-time guardrail, lint to stop regressions.

questions.contextHtml: A 14-engineer mobile team (8 Android, 5 iOS, 1 QA lead). The Android lead proposes Kotlin Multiplatform for networking, auth and domain logic, saying it saves 30% of feature time. iOS engineers object: "we will debug Kotlin stack traces, Swift API will be ugly, our build gets slower." The CTO asks you for a recommendation by Friday. App: 900k MAU, features ship simultaneously on both platforms, 2 backend-driven rules engines duplicated on both sides with divergent bugs (7 parity bugs last quarter).
questions.promptHtml: What do you recommend and how do you run it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "KMP is stable, so adopt it everywhere." Ignores people and the actual duplicated pain.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is duplicated and costly (the two rules engines)? Who owns the shared module? Is iOS willing to review Kotlin? What is the current CI and release setup for iOS? Is there a UI sharing wish or only logic?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A. The pain is the parity bugs; target exactly that.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Sharing pure logic with high parity risk gives the best value; (b) the main risk is the iOS team's experience, not the technology; (c) sharing networking/DI broadly gives little.
  4. How I'd verify: A 6-week pilot with one rules engine moved to a shared module; measure parity bugs, iOS build time, crash-free rates, developer survey.
  5. Root cause: The problem is duplicated logic and divergent behavior; sharing is one possible tool. KMP is stable for sharing logic and Compose Multiplatform for iOS is stable as of 2025 (from official site, verify current status), but readiness does not decide fit.
  6. Fix: Recommend a scoped pilot: share the rules engine only, expose a narrow Swift-friendly API (verify use of SKIE or Swift export options), co-own the module with an iOS engineer, keep UI native, gate by explicit exit criteria. Document expect/actual usage and keep platform code minimal.
// commonMain: no Android/iOS imports
class PricingRules(private val clock: Clock) {
    fun quote(cart: Cart): Quote { /* pure logic, tested in commonTest */ }
}
  1. Prevention: Decision record with metrics and a stop condition: if iOS build time grows more than X% or the pilot misses parity targets, stop.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not share UI in phase one; I'd not mandate adoption over iOS objections, as ownership is what makes it work. KMP costs: Gradle/Xcode integration, binary size, interop debugging.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• iOS lead refuses completely. → Then use a shared spec and test vectors (contract tests) as a cheaper fix to parity.
  • The pilot succeeded; what next? → Expand module by module based on duplicated-bug cost.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A pilot on pricing cut parity bugs to near zero; networking sharing was dropped because Ktor offered little over each platform's native stack for that team.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: All-in or all-out.
  • Hire: Scoped pilot with metrics.
  • Strong hire: Addresses team ownership, interop API, exit criteria, and offers a non-KMP fallback.

questions.promptHtml: How do you decide which layer or scope owns a piece of state: Composable, state holder, ViewModel, repository, app scope, or disk?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most scenario bugs (stale data, lost state, leaks) are ownership mistakes. Seniors have a rule, not a vibe.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I ask who needs it, how long it must live, and whether it must survive process death. UI-only, ephemeral state stays in the composable; screen logic state goes into a ViewModel; data shared across screens lives in a repository backed by disk; user session data lives in a session scope that dies on logout; and anything the user would be angry to lose goes to disk."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
State kind                      Owner                      Survives
Scroll position, animation      Composable (remember)      recomposition only
Text field draft                rememberSaveable/VM        config + process death
Screen UiState (derived)        ViewModel                  config change
Entity data (cart, profile)     Repository + Room          process death
Session identity, tokens        Session scope              until logout
App config/flags                app scope + defaults       process
Pending writes                  Outbox (disk)              process death

Rule of thumb: single writer, many readers. The owner exposes immutable state (StateFlow) and accepts intents. Everything else derives. If two components both mutate the same value, there is a bug waiting.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Single owner, many readers
class CartRepository(private val dao: CartDao) {
    fun observeCart(): Flow<List<CartItem>> = dao.observeAll().map { it.map(CartEntity::toDomain) }
    suspend fun add(item: CartItem) = dao.insert(item.toEntity())
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using the ViewModel as a data cache shared across screens.
  • Putting user data in @Singleton (see logout leak).
  • Using SavedStateHandle as a database.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does selected-tab state live? → Navigation/back stack or a hoisted state holder; it is UI state.
  2. Where does a draft message live? → rememberSaveable for small text, disk for large drafts.
  3. Shared filter between two screens? → A small shared holder or repository-level setting with a clear owner.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "ViewModel holds state." Senior: assigns every kind of state a lifetime owner and a single writer, and uses a table.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Stale cart badge and logout leak incidents share this root: copies and wrong lifetime.

questions.contextHtml: A new VP says: "The app is a mess. Estimate a full rewrite to Compose, modules, Clean Architecture, and KMP." Current app: 7 years old, 380k lines, 50% Views/XML, 1.8M DAU, crash-free 99.4%, build time 22 min, 18 engineers. Roadmap has 3 committed features this half. Engineers are excited; the PM is nervous.
questions.promptHtml: How do you respond?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Sure, 9 months." Or "No, rewrites always fail" with no alternative.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What pain exactly (build time, crash rate, velocity, hiring)? What outcomes and by when? What is the cost of delay on features? Is leadership willing to fund parallel tracks?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; prevent a premature commitment by turning the ask into measurable problems.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The real pains are build time and regression rate, solvable without a rewrite; (b) most screens do not need rewriting, only the hot ones; (c) "mess" is partly a perception from a few bad areas.
  4. How I'd verify: Churn and bug heatmap (git history crossed with crash data); build scan; survey of developer friction; identify top 10 screens by traffic and by change frequency.
  5. Root cause: The request bundles four separate migrations (UI toolkit, modularization, layering, multiplatform) with different payoffs and risks.
  6. Fix: Propose a strangler plan in stages with exit criteria: (1) build and CI hygiene (config cache, remote cache), (2) new screens in Compose with interop, (3) extract modules along hot seams, (4) layering only where the god classes live, (5) evaluate KMP separately. Reserve 20% capacity, track metrics (build time, crash-free, lead time), reassess each quarter. Present cost of each option, including the rewrite estimate with risk range (rewrites of this size commonly take 2x estimate; state it as my experience, not data).
  7. Prevention: An ADR that records the decision and the metrics that would justify a bigger step.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not freeze features for a rewrite; I'd not promise a date; I'd not start four migrations at once.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• VP insists on rewrite. → Offer a time-boxed spike on one vertical slice as evidence.
  • Engineers want KMP now. → Separate decision; see the adoption pilot approach.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "rewrite" dropped to a 6-month hot-path migration; build time fell from 22 to 11 minutes by quarter two with no UI changes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Accepts or rejects blindly.
  • Hire: Splits into stages with metrics.
  • Strong hire: Evidence-led (churn x crash), executive framing, reassessment checkpoints.

questions.contextHtml: A seed-stage startup, 5 engineers (2 Android), MVP in 10 weeks, uncertain product direction, 3 screens may be dropped. The CTO asks you to "design the Android architecture." One engineer proposes 12 modules, use cases for everything, and MVI with a custom framework.
questions.promptHtml: What architecture do you propose and what do you defer?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Presents the large-company reference architecture.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Offline needs? Number of backend teams? Expected team growth in 12 months? Compliance? Which parts are core to the product?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; set principles first: optimize for change and delivery speed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Premature structure costs more than it protects when product direction may shift; but a few cheap boundaries pay off immediately.
  4. How I'd verify: Revisit at 3 months: build time, number of engineers, number of features, pain points.
  5. Root cause: N/A.
  6. Fix (proposal): Single :app module with package-by-feature; Compose; one ViewModel per screen exposing StateFlow<UiState>; repositories only where there is real data logic; Hilt for DI (standard, minimal cost); Retrofit/Ktor + Room only as needed; navigation with type-safe routes. Boundaries that are cheap now: DTO to UI model mapping, repository interface per data domain, no Android types in ViewModels, and dispatchers injected. Defer: multi-module, use-case layer, custom MVI, KMP.
app/
  feature/home   (Screen, ViewModel, UiState)
  feature/chat
  data/          (repositories, api, db)
  core/          (design system, util)
  1. Prevention: Write the migration triggers into an ADR: split into modules when build exceeds N minutes or teams exceed M; add use cases when logic is shared between two ViewModels.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not build custom frameworks; I'd not skip tests entirely, I'd test ViewModels and repositories only.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Investor wants iOS in 3 months. → Keep domain logic in plain Kotlin classes to leave KMP open, but do not adopt it yet.
  • You grow to 15 engineers in a year. → Triggers fire: extract core and 2-3 feature modules first.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A startup shipped on 2 modules and added modules at 12 engineers with a 3-week effort because package-by-feature made seams visible.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Enterprise architecture.
  • Hire: Simple structure with a few boundaries.
  • Strong hire: Named triggers for evolution and cheap boundaries rationale.

questions.contextHtml: A one-line change in :core:model (adding a nullable field to User) triggers recompilation of 60 of 85 modules, local incremental build 7 minutes (previously 40 s for typical changes). Build scan: :feature:*:compileDebugKotlin all executed with "classpath changed". Build files mostly use api(project(":core:model")).
questions.promptHtml: Why does one change fan out and what do you do about it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Gradle is slow; upgrade Gradle."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it ABI change (public API) or just implementation? Is :core:model depended on by all? Is Kotlin incremental compile enabled? Are annotation processors involved?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Batch such changes; build only needed modules (:feature:x:assembleDebug) while fixing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) api configuration exposes :core:model transitively to all consumers' compile classpaths so ABI changes ripple; (b) User is public and used everywhere, so adding a field changes the ABI that dependents compile against; (c) KAPT stubs rerun.
  4. How I'd verify: Build scan "Build timeline" and "Task inputs" to see "classpath changed"; ./gradlew :feature:x:dependencies; check whether modules actually need it.
  5. Root cause: A very central model module with wide exposure, in which any ABI change invalidates the compile classpath of all consumers. api makes it worse by leaking it transitively.
  6. Fix: Use implementation unless the type appears in the module's public signatures; split :core:model into smaller domain-specific model modules; keep leaf types behind feature-specific models; mark internals internal; consider ABI-stable interfaces. Kotlin's compile avoidance reduces recompiles only for non-ABI changes.
dependencies {
    implementation(projects.core.model)     // not api, unless exposed in public signatures
}
  1. Prevention: Dependency-analysis plugin (verify tool) to flag wrong api usage; track "modules rebuilt per commit" metric.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not convert everything to implementation blindly (compile errors for exposed types); I'd not add -Xno-... flags without reading docs.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Adding a private function in User? → Not an ABI change; should not trigger downstream compile (verify with scan).
  • Fan-in module with 60 dependents is inevitable? → Keep it small and stable; push volatile things out.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Splitting one 300-class model module into 5 cut average modules rebuilt per PR from 52 to 11.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "Upgrade Gradle."
  • Hire: Explains api vs implementation and ABI.
  • Strong hire: Splits the hub, adds measurement and tooling.

questions.contextHtml: Cold start p90 regressed from 1.4 s to 2.3 s on mid-range devices after DI was extended. Perfetto trace: 620 ms on main thread inside Application.onCreate on Hilt_App.onCreate and eager @Singleton constructors that open a Room DB, create an OkHttp client with a 10 MB cache, initialize analytics SDKs, and read DataStore with runBlocking. Android vitals flags slow cold start in 14% of sessions.
questions.promptHtml: Find the causes and restore startup time without breaking dependency graph correctness.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch to Koin, it's lighter." Misattributes cost to the framework; the work is the same.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is on the critical path to first frame? Which initializers are required before UI? Release or debug trace?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move non-critical SDK init off the main thread/after first frame; stop runBlocking on main.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Eager work in constructors of singletons injected into Application; (b) runBlocking on DataStore blocking main; (c) DI graph itself (generated code, usually small relative to the work it triggers); (d) reflection-heavy libs.
  4. How I'd verify: Perfetto / system trace with custom trace sections; Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric; Baseline Profile comparison.
  5. Root cause: Constructors doing I/O; with Dagger/Hilt, construction time is where cost surfaces because instances are created on first injection.
  6. Fix: Constructors do no work; inject Lazy<T> / Provider<T> for heavy objects used later; initialize SDKs with App Startup or a background scope; read the first-frame-needed config asynchronously with a splash-safe default.
class HomeActivity : ComponentActivity() {
    @Inject lateinit var analytics: dagger.Lazy<Analytics>   // created at first use
}

Generate a Baseline Profile for startup path (verify Macrobenchmark setup). 7. Prevention: Startup Macrobenchmark in CI with budget (fail PR on p50 regression > X ms); StrictMode on main; review rule: no I/O in constructors or init. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not delay initialization that crash reporting needs; I'd not make every dependency lazy (hides latency to first use).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Lazy moves cost to first screen interaction. → Warm up in the background after first frame.
  • Is Hilt cost from aggregation? → That is a build-time cost; runtime is generated direct code.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: One eagerly built analytics singleton had a 200 ms disk read; after lazy init and background warmup, p90 returned to 1.5 s.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames the DI framework.
  • Hire: Finds constructor work and defers it.
  • Strong hire: Uses traces, adds regression budget, explains Lazy vs warmup trade-off.

questions.contextHtml:
Customers report double charges: "I tapped Pay once, got two orders." Rate 0.3% of checkouts, roughly 450 per day at 150k checkouts/day. Server logs show two POST /orders with different request timestamps 400-900 ms apart. Code:

class CheckoutViewModel(private val repo: OrderRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _ui = MutableStateFlow(CheckoutUi())
    val ui = _ui.asStateFlow()

    fun onPayClicked() {
        if (_ui.value.loading) return
        viewModelScope.launch {
            _ui.update { it.copy(loading = true) }
            repo.placeOrder()     // retrofit POST, retried by OkHttp on connection failure
            _ui.update { it.copy(loading = false, done = true) }
        }
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find all the causes of duplicates.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Only "disable the button." Misses the network and server side.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are the POSTs from the same device? Is retry on connection failure enabled? Does the server support an idempotency key? Are users double-tapping or are retries involved?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side dedupe window by (user, cart hash) as a stopgap; disable the retry for non-idempotent POST.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) OkHttp retryOnConnectionFailure resends the POST after a timeout when the first reached the server; (b) the guard loading is set inside the launched coroutine, so two taps in the same frame both pass before the update (check-then-act race on main thread is less likely but launch is queued with Dispatchers.Main, not Main.immediate); (c) process restoration re-triggering; (d) user retry after timeout.
  4. How I'd verify: Server request IDs and user agent; client log of taps; reproduce with adb input tap twice rapidly; OkHttp event listener for retries.
  5. Root cause: No idempotency. The guard is racy (state set after dispatch), and transport-level retry duplicates a non-idempotent call.
  6. Fix: Set loading synchronously before launch; generate an idempotency key per checkout attempt, persisted with the attempt, sent as a header; server dedupes by key; treat timeouts as unknown and reconcile by querying by key.
fun onPayClicked() {
    if (_ui.getAndUpdate { it.copy(loading = true) }.loading) return   // atomic check-and-set
    val key = attemptKey ?: UUID.randomUUID().toString().also { attemptKey = it }
    viewModelScope.launch { repo.placeOrder(idempotencyKey = key) /* ... */ }
}
  1. Prevention: Contract test that a duplicated POST with the same key yields one order; chaos test with dropped responses; alert on duplicate rate.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not rely on UI disabling alone; I'd not retry POST without a key.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• App killed after sending but before response. → The persisted key allows reconciliation on restart.
  • Key reuse across different carts? → Key is per attempt, reset when the cart changes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Duplicate orders dropped from 0.3% to under 0.01% after idempotency keys, even before the UI fix.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Disable button.
  • Hire: Identifies retry and race and adds keys.
  • Strong hire: Reconciliation after unknown outcome, persisted key, tests and alerting.

questions.contextHtml:
Support: "App says 'No internet connection' but my Wi-Fi works." 2.1% of sessions show the offline banner while telemetry shows the device is online. Backend had a 40-minute partial outage returning HTTP 503 for 30% of calls. The repository:

suspend fun load(): Result<Feed> = try {
    Result.success(api.feed().toDomain())
} catch (e: Exception) {
    Result.failure(e)
}
// ViewModel
.onFailure { _ui.value = UiState.Error("No internet connection") }
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong with the error architecture and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Change the message text." The model is wrong, not the text.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What failure kinds exist (no network, timeout, 4xx, 5xx, parsing)? What can the user do for each? Does cache exist to show stale data?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the message to a generic "Something went wrong, retry"; show cached feed if present.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) All failures collapse into one UI message; (b) catch (e: Exception) also swallows CancellationException, breaking coroutine cancellation (spot-the-second-bug); (c) the HTTP errors are thrown as HttpException and treated as connectivity.
  4. How I'd verify: Log exception class per failure; unit test with MockWebServer returning 503 and assert the mapped error.
  5. Root cause: Errors are not modeled; the data layer leaks "an exception happened" and the UI guesses a cause.
  6. Fix: Define domain errors, map in the repository, rethrow cancellation, and let the UI map to user messages:
sealed interface DataError { object Offline : DataError; object Timeout : DataError
    data class Server(val code: Int) : DataError; object Unknown : DataError }

suspend fun load(): Either<DataError, Feed> = try { Right(api.feed().toDomain()) }
catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
catch (e: IOException) { Left(if (e is SocketTimeoutException) DataError.Timeout else DataError.Offline) }
catch (e: HttpException) { Left(DataError.Server(e.code())) }

(Either is any sealed result type; the Kotlin stdlib Result is also acceptable if wrapped consistently.) Show stale cache plus a non-blocking banner when available. 7. Prevention: Tests per error class; lint/detekt for swallowed CancellationException; telemetry counting error kinds. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not put Retrofit HttpException in UI; I'd not model every HTTP code individually.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 401 mid-session? → Handled by the auth layer (token refresh/logout); the repository maps it to Unauthorized for the UI.
  • Retry policy? → Only for idempotent requests, with backoff; surface to user after N failures.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "no internet" banner during a backend outage generated thousands of tickets to the wrong team.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Edits message text.
  • Hire: Sealed error model and mapping at boundary.
  • Strong hire: Catches cancellation trap, stale-data UX, and test strategy.

questions.contextHtml:
Compose app with bottom navigation (Home, Search, Profile). QA bug: scroll position and the nested Search filters reset when switching tabs; also pressing Back from Profile's detail goes to Home instead of Profile's root. Crash: IllegalArgumentException: No destination with ID once per 5k sessions. Code on tab click:

navController.navigate(tab.route) {
    popUpTo(navController.graph.startDestinationId)
}

Navigation Compose 2.8, type-safe routes.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Store scroll in the ViewModel and call it a day."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are tabs separate nested graphs? Do tabs share ViewModel scope? What should happen on re-tapping the active tab?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Apply the standard options below; ship as a patch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) popUpTo without saveState = true and restoreState = true discards tab back stacks; (b) missing launchSingleTop; (c) tabs are flat destinations rather than nested graphs so the stack of each tab is not independent; (d) the crash from a stale route id after a refactor (red herring unless correlated with version).
  4. How I'd verify: Log navController.currentBackStack; use the navigation test APIs; reproduce tab hopping with a detail screen on each tab.
  5. Root cause: Without saveState, popping up to start removes entries and state; no per-tab back stack.
  6. Fix:
navController.navigate(tab.route) {
    popUpTo(navController.graph.findStartDestination().id) { saveState = true }
    launchSingleTop = true
    restoreState = true
}

Make each tab a nested graph (navigation<HomeGraph>(startDestination = HomeRoot)), so detail screens belong to their tab; scope tab-level ViewModels to the graph entry if they must survive tab switches. For the crash, verify routes are the typed classes, not strings. 7. Prevention: Navigation UI tests for tab switching and back; a shared bottom-bar helper function used everywhere. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not keep every tab composed at once (memory); saved state is enough.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Re-tapping the active tab should scroll to top. → Handle reselect in the UI and send a signal or pop to the root.
  • Back from tab root? → Define it: go to Home first or exit.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Dropping restoreState was the cause of a long-standing "Search forgets filters" bug filed under five tickets.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Persist in ViewModel only.
  • Hire: Correct navigate options.
  • Strong hire: Nested graphs, per-tab back stack, and tests.

questions.subtopic: Saved state compatibility across app updates
questions.promptHtml: After an app update, a user returns to a backgrounded app and it crashes while restoring. What architecture decisions make restored state safe across versions?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Update plus process death is a real combination: the system can restore saved state written by the old version into new code. Few candidates have thought about it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Saved instance state and persisted data have schema, and old data meets new code. I keep saved state small and tolerant: nullable with defaults, no custom class serialization if avoidable, route arguments that are primitives, a version field when needed, and I treat restore failures as 'start fresh' instead of crash."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Cases: (1) Bundle saved by version N restored in N+1 after a package replacement: normally the app update kills the process and the task's saved state is generally discarded, but behaviors vary and should be treated as unverified (verify per OS version); (2) persisted state in DataStore/Room/SharedPreferences, which definitely crosses versions; (3) back stack routes serialized with kotlinx.serialization: renaming a field or making it required breaks decoding of old entries.

Serialized route v1: {"productId":"42"}
Route v2 adds: val source: String   // required, no default => decode failure for old data
Route v2 safe: val source: String = "unknown"
