Rules: add fields with defaults; never repurpose a field; use @SerialName to keep names stable; migrate persisted data (Room migrations, DataStore migrations); treat unknown enum values as a fallback; wrap restore in defensive handling.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Serializable
data class ProductDetail(
    val productId: String,
    val source: String = "unknown",       // new in v2, default keeps old entries valid
)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding a required field to a route class.
  • Saving a Serializable model class with default Java serialization.
  • Not testing upgrade with real saved data.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you test it? → Install version N, navigate, background, upgrade via adb install -r, return; plus unit tests that decode stored JSON samples.
  2. Enum value added by server? → Use a safe fallback value.
  3. Persisted DataStore proto change? → Add fields with defaults; use migrations.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE ignores it. Senior treats routes and persisted state as versioned contracts.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A crash cluster appearing only for the first day after a release is a typical sign of old state meeting new code.

questions.contextHtml: The app is adding multi-account support (up to 5 accounts, instant switching) for a messaging product with 3M DAU and sync via a background service. Current design: one @Singleton per data service, DB app.db, DataStore per app. Product wants zero logout, and background sync continuing for inactive accounts. Past incident: cross-user data leak. Security and privacy review required.
questions.promptHtml: Design the architecture for multi-account without leaks or complexity explosion.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Clear everything and reload on switch." Violates instant switching and background sync.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which data is per account (messages, settings) vs global (theme)? Memory budget with 5 active accounts? Push notification routing per account? Does sync run simultaneously for all?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; set the isolation invariant: no component may read user data without an account context.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Main risks are shared singletons holding data, shared DB/files, caches (HTTP, images), and worker tasks without account identity.
  4. How I'd verify: Inventory singletons and storage locations; threat model; instrumented tests that switch accounts and assert no cross-emission.
  5. Root cause: N/A; design.
  6. Fix: An AccountScope container per account id: per-account database file (db_<id>), DataStore file, OkHttp client with its own auth interceptor and cache dir, and a CoroutineScope cancelled when the account is removed. App-scoped singletons hold only config. An AccountManager exposes activeAccount: StateFlow<AccountId> and fun scope(id): AccountScope. UI-scoped ViewModels receive the active scope via a provider and restart collection on switch (flatMapLatest). Background work (WorkManager) takes accountId as input data and builds its own scope, never reads "current account".
val messages: StateFlow<List<Msg>> = accountManager.active
    .flatMapLatest { id -> accountManager.scope(id).messageRepo.observe() }
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyList())

With Hilt, the scope container is a hand-built graph or Dagger subcomponent behind an entry point (custom Hilt components are not supported; verify). 7. Prevention: Account id required in all repository constructors (compile-time safety); lint rule banning getCurrentUser() globals; leak tests; privacy review of notifications. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not hold 5 full in-memory graphs; instantiate lazily and release inactive accounts' heavy caches. Cost: more files, more complexity in sync.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Memory pressure with 5 accounts. → Dispose inactive scopes' in-memory caches but keep DB.
  • Push arrives for inactive account. → Notification handler resolves account scope by id from payload.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The first design shared an image cache; a cached avatar for the wrong account appeared in a notification. Per-account cache directories fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Clear and reload.
  • Hire: Per-account scope and storage isolation.
  • Strong hire: Background work identity, memory strategy, compile-time enforcement, privacy review.

questions.contextHtml: The Android team grows from 8 to 40 engineers in 12 months, split into 5 squads. Currently: 28 modules, one :app that depends on all, weekly releases. Symptoms already: merge conflicts in AppModule, nav graph, and strings.xml (30 per week), PR review wait 2 days p50, a squad's crash blocks the whole release, CI queue time 40 min.
questions.promptHtml: What do you change in architecture and process to make 40 engineers productive?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "More modules." Without ownership or contracts it multiplies conflicts.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which squad owns which product areas? How are releases structured (train vs per-squad)? What is the current build and test time? What conflicts occur where?
  2. Immediate mitigation: CODEOWNERS and merge queue; split the biggest conflict hotspots (registration of features).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Central registration files are contention points; (b) ownership boundaries do not match module boundaries (Conway's law); (c) CI capacity, not code; (d) a shared release train couples all squads.
  4. How I'd verify: Git churn on top conflicted files; PR cycle-time stats; module ownership map vs squad map; CI queue metrics.
  5. Root cause: Structure mirrors the old team, not the new one; shared files centralize change.
  6. Fix: Align modules with squads (feature modules owned per squad with api/impl), with contracts in api modules; replace central registration with DI multibindings (@IntoSet/@IntoMap) so each feature registers itself; each squad owns its strings and resources in its module; convention plugins for consistent build setup; feature flags to decouple deploy from release; merge queue, remote cache, affected-module CI; dependency rules enforced in CI.
@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
abstract class OrdersNavModule {
    @Binds @IntoSet abstract fun nav(impl: OrdersNavContributor): NavContributor
}
  1. Prevention: Ownership map in CODEOWNERS; architecture review for new modules; metrics: cycle time, conflict count, CI time.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not create a module per screen; I'd not give squads full autonomy over shared core without a platform team owner.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Platform team versus feature teams? → A small platform squad owns core, build logic, design system.
  • A squad's bug blocks the release? → Flags plus per-feature kill switches; consider release trains with cut-offs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Moving to multibinding registration removed the main contention file; weekly conflicts dropped from 30 to about 4.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Add modules.
  • Hire: Ownership-aligned modules and self-registration.
  • Strong hire: Combines architecture, flags, CI, and org design with metrics.

questions.contextHtml: CI unit tests: 6% of runs fail, different tests each time (ProfileViewModelTest, SyncRepositoryTest). Re-run passes. Stack excerpts: UncompletedCoroutinesError, IllegalStateException: Module with the Main dispatcher had failed to initialize, and an assertion seeing data from a previous test. Code uses Dispatchers.IO hard-coded in repositories and a Hilt @Singleton fake reused across tests via a static object.
questions.promptHtml: Find the flakiness sources and fix them architecturally.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add retries or Thread.sleep to the tests."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are tests run in parallel? Are Main dispatcher setup/teardown done per test? Are there static fakes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Quarantine the flakiest tests with a tracking issue, do not auto-retry silently.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Hard-coded Dispatchers.IO escapes the test scheduler, so coroutines finish at nondeterministic times; (b) missing Dispatchers.setMain/resetMain rule; (c) shared mutable static state across tests; (d) real time (delay, System.currentTimeMillis).
  4. How I'd verify: Run the suite 50 times in a loop with random order; --tests single repeated; look for dispatcher thread names in logs.
  5. Root cause: Architecture does not let tests control threads, time and state.
  6. Fix: Inject dispatchers, use StandardTestDispatcher/runTest, a MainDispatcherRule, per-test fresh fakes, and inject a Clock.
class SyncRepository @Inject constructor(
    private val api: Api, @IoDispatcher private val io: CoroutineDispatcher,
) { suspend fun sync() = withContext(io) { api.sync() } }

class MainDispatcherRule(private val d: TestDispatcher = StandardTestDispatcher()) : TestWatcher() {
    override fun starting(description: Description) = Dispatchers.setMain(d)
    override fun finished(description: Description) = Dispatchers.resetMain()
}
  1. Prevention: Lint/detekt rule against hard-coded Dispatchers.* in production classes (verify availability); flaky test dashboard; random test order.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not mock everything; fakes are more robust. I'd not use runBlocking in tests as a workaround.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• UI tests flaky on animations? → Disable animations in test config and use idling/sync mechanisms.
  • Should tests share a Hilt component? → Each test gets a fresh component via Hilt testing rules.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Flaky rate fell from 6% to under 0.3% after injecting dispatchers and removing three static fakes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Retries or sleep.
  • Hire: Injected dispatchers and test scheduler.
  • Strong hire: Static state, clock injection, order randomization and quarantine policy.

questions.contextHtml: Product: "Make the app work offline within 6 weeks." App: field-service app, 25k technicians, 2 backend teams, 60 screens mostly CRUD forms (work orders, photos, signatures). Connectivity: 15% of shifts in low-signal sites. Current architecture: ViewModels call Retrofit repositories directly; no local DB. Team of 6 Android engineers.
questions.promptHtml: How do you turn this ambiguous request into a plan and scope it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add Room and cache everything." Ignores writes, conflicts and the 6-week limit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does "work offline" mean: read cached data or create/edit offline? Which screens are critical? Conflict rules if two people edit a work order? How long offline (hours/days)? Photo size/storage limits? Compliance on stored data?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; write a scoped definition with the PM: Tier 1 read-only offline for assigned work orders; Tier 2 offline create/edit for 3 key flows; the rest later.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Writes plus conflict resolution are the hard part; (b) uploading photos needs a reliable queue; (c) backend lacks idempotency or versioning; (d) migrating ViewModel-to-API code needs repository seams.
  4. How I'd verify: Measure real offline duration; review API for idempotency and version fields; spike one flow end to end.
  5. Root cause: N/A; scope definition.
  6. Fix (plan): Weeks 1-2: introduce repositories with Room as the single source of truth for the Tier 1 entities, UI observes Room via Flow. Weeks 3-5: outbox table for writes (operation, payload, idempotency key, status), WorkManager uploader with backoff and constraints (details in the persistence track), last-write-wins or server-version conflict rule agreed with backend. Week 6: hardening, offline banners, sync status UI, test in airplane mode. Explicit non-goals recorded.
@Entity data class OutboxOp(@PrimaryKey val id: String, val type: String, val payload: String,
    val attempts: Int = 0, val state: String = "PENDING")
  1. Prevention: Offline test suite with network toggle; telemetry for outbox size and sync failures; contracts with backend on idempotency.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I'd not promise full offline for 60 screens in 6 weeks; I'd not build a generic sync engine; I'd not hide sync status from users.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two technicians edit the same order offline. → Version field plus conflict UI for critical fields, merge for independent fields.
  • Storage limit for photos? → Compress, queue size cap, upload on Wi-Fi when allowed.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The team shipped Tier 1 on time; Tier 2 revealed the backend lacked idempotency, which became the long pole.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "Add Room."
  • Hire: Clarifies scope, introduces outbox and Room as truth.
  • Strong hire: Tiers scope, addresses conflicts and backend contracts, sets non-goals and metrics.
